editorial.titleTr: President Leaves Door Open on Graft Case Despite Ruling Out Reelection Bid
summaryTr: President Lee Jae-myung clarifies he has no intention to seek reelection and acknowledges responsibility for declining approval ratings
Double standard emerges as he requests deletion of charges dismissal clause while maintaining necessity for special prosecutor
Editorial urges integrative leadership and actions aligned with public expectations
editorial.bodyTr: President Lee Jae-myung announced he has no intention of seeking reelection and acknowledged responsibility for declining approval ratings, offering an apology. President Lee Jae-myung requested the deletion of provisions related to the dismissal of charges in the special prosecution law on fabricated indictments, while maintaining the necessity of a special prosecution. The editorial pointed out personnel controversies and divisive remarks, emphasizing that he must demonstrate unity through actions that meet the public's expectations.

summaryTr: President Lee Jae-myung blames previous administration as real estate market remains undefeated
Seoul housing prices surge sharply while government diagnosis disconnects from reality
Inadequate measures for monthly rent tenants and farmers, tax reform also falls short
editorials.bodyTr: President Lee Jae-myung spoke of the myth of real estate being a fail-safe investment and said that policies from the previous administration exacerbated the housing price problem. The article criticized the government for deflecting responsibility despite the serious rise in Seoul housing prices and for offering a market diagnosis that does not match reality. The article pointed out that in the controversy surrounding tax reform and a comprehensive survey of farmland, there are insufficient measures to appease jeonse and monthly rent tenants and farmers.

editorial.titleTr: Editorial: He Confirms He Won't Seek Reelection, but Appeals to Supporters Instead of the People
summaryTr: President Lee Jae-myung officially confirmed he has no intention to seek reelection.
He demanded the deletion of the special prosecutor's authority to withdraw indictments, but concrete results have fallen short.
The lack of will for state affairs reform has left prospects for a policy turning point uncertain.
editorial.bodyTr: President Lee Jae-myung has officially confirmed through a press conference that he has no intention of seeking reelection and demanded the removal of the special prosecutor's authority to drop charges. However, he has taken a passive stance on changes to state policy direction regarding real estate and other matters, as well as on institutional reform. The situation remains unclear regarding the future direction of state administration, as he also failed to clarify the status of Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won.

summaryTr: Seoul Administrative Court cancels severe disciplinary action against soldier with passive stance during martial law

editorials.bodyTr: The Seoul Administrative Court ruled that severe disciplinary measures imposed on a soldier who took a passive stance while carrying out unlawful orders during the December 3 martial law should be overturned. This ruling, while taking into account the unique nature of the military, clearly established that disciplinary action is unjust when there is no active participation, and it carries significant social implications calling for the Defense Ministry to reconsider its disciplinary handling.

editorials.titleTr: Editorial: How Can We Talk of Unification Without Building a Single School for North Korean Defector Youth?
summaryTr: Construction of Yeomyeong School, an alternative school for North Korean defector youth, has been blocked due to resident opposition.
Concerns over falling property values are hindering social inclusion.
It is urgent to fulfill the government's responsibility in unification education.
editorials.bodyTr: Yeomyeong School, an alternative school for North Korean refugee youth, is pursuing construction of a new campus building in Gayang-dong, Gangseo-gu, but faces difficulties due to resident opposition driven by concerns over falling property values. Despite the school having secured funding and receiving government support, it struggles to convince the community. This situation underscores the urgent need for public responsibility and attention toward social inclusion and unification education.

editorial.titleTr: Fed Reverses Course After 3 Years of Tightening...High Rates and Inflation Headwinds Loom
summaryTr: The U.S. Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years, shifting to a tightening stance.
South Korea is also facing rising waves of high interest rates and high inflation amid elevated oil prices and inflationary pressures.
Government expansionary fiscal policy fuels inflation, making strict budget control by the National Assembly necessary.
editorial.bodyTr: The United States has returned to financial tightening after more than three years. The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to an annual 3.75-4% on the 16th. This marks the first rate increase in 3 years and 2 months since July 2023. The decision was unanimous among the 12 members of the Federal Open Market Committee. Fed Chair Kevin Walsh stated the reason for the increase: "Inflation is too high and has been for too long." Though President Donald Trump pressured the Fed ahead of midterm elections to lower rates "below 1%," the Fed reaffirmed its commitment to price stability and even left open the possibility of additional rate increases within the year. The direct trigger for the shift toward tightening is the sharp spike in international oil prices, driven by prolonged Middle East tensions, which have pushed crude above $100 per barrel. As rising oil prices amplify inflation and compound concerns about America's massive fiscal deficit and mounting interest burdens on national debt, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has surpassed 5%. This is the highest level since 2007. As Japan's 10-year bond yield also jumped to the 3% range for the first time in 30 years, the Bank of Japan is expected to raise rates further today. The world now stands at the threshold of major tightening. These rising rates will push up corporate loans, corporate bonds, and mortgage rates alike, tightening the money supply for businesses and households. South Korea too faces mounting waves of high interest rates and high inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield has exceeded 4.5%, and consumer prices have remained in the 3% range for two consecutive months. Households that purchased homes and invested in stocks during the low-interest era through maximum leverage and debt investment are now facing a direct hit from surging interest payments. In this situation, the government is compiling a record 821 trillion won budget for next year, embarking on unprecedented fiscal expansion. Riding expectations of a semiconductor boom, the budget has been increased 12.8% from this year. Reckless discretionary spending will ultimately stoke inflation and weaken the economic structure. On the 6th ahead of the Chuseok holiday, citizens purchase apples at Cheongnyangni Comprehensive Market in Dongdaemun-gu, Seoul. According to data from the National Statistical Office portal on that day, pear prices rose 8.4% year-on-year and crucian carp rose 8.5%, while key Chuseok table items like eggs, domestic beef, seasoned vegetables, and glass noodles showed upward trends, increasing the burden on holiday shopping baskets. America's shift toward tightening is a warning to break free from the momentum of the low-interest era. The Bank of Korea is also expected to raise its benchmark rate once more within the year. As waves of high interest rates and high inflation mount, households, businesses, and government must all take action in debt management and prepare for shocks. In particular, careful legislative oversight of the budget is needed to ensure government spending does not fall out of step with the central bank's price stabilization efforts. There can be no stability in people's livelihoods without price stability.

editorial.title: Costly capital
editorial.body: Higher borrowing costs demand reforms that lift productivity, strengthen finances Cheap money has enjoyed a remarkably long run. Its retirement is now harder to deny, forcing South Korea to rethink policies built around the assumption that capital will remain cheap. This week, the 10-year US Treasury yield broke above 5 percent while the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4 percent, its first increase since July 2023. For more than two decades, cheap capital, energy and labor helped economies absorb inefficiencies that otherwise would have been costly. As that cushion shrinks, the nation should stop building policy around the expectation that rates will soon return to their old lows. Long-term yields are being shaped by more than near-term inflation. Oil above $100 a barrel is adding to price pressures as conflict persists in the Middle East. The vast sums being poured into artificial intelligence infrastructure are also competing for global savings. US fiscal policy is another strain. Gross public debt has climbed above 110 percent of gross domestic product, and investors are demanding a larger premium to hold long-dated government bonds. The special advantage once enjoyed by Treasurys as exceptionally liquid and safe assets has also weakened. There is a tempting shortcut. Governments can issue more short-term debt to avoid locking in today's elevated long-term yields. But that merely brings the problem closer. With more debt maturing sooner, refinancing becomes costlier if rates stay high. A changing investor base, with more price-sensitive and leveraged participants in bond markets, can make benchmark yields more volatile. Korea is already feeling the shock. The 10-year Treasury bond yield has risen above 4.6 percent, reaching its highest level since October 2022. Higher government bond yields eventually feed into corporate borrowing costs and bank lending rates, squeezing businesses and households. The Bank of Korea has also tightened, raising its policy rate to 3 percent over two consecutive meetings in July and August. It was the first back-to-back tightening since January 2023, when the BOK completed a rate-hike cycle that began in April 2022. The gap with the Fed has widened to as much as 1 percentage point, with a weaker won and heavy household leverage adding to the strain. Yet simply matching every Fed move would be poor monetary policy. The BOK should set clear conditions for further increases and weigh their timing against domestic inflation, exchange rates and credit conditions. Household credit has already exceeded 2,000 trillion won ($1.45 trillion), and corporate debt is nearing that scale. Higher interest expenses will weigh most heavily on borrowers with little room to absorb them. Financial support should therefore be selective. Extending loans indefinitely can conceal losses rather than resolve them. Fiscal policy faces its own burden. Large-scale government borrowing can put further upward pressure on market rates, and interest payments consume more of the budget. Korea should trim nonessential spending to preserve primary fiscal stability. When capital is expensive, competitiveness depends on the output generated by each unit of investment. That calls for regulatory reform to lower barriers to market entry, give labor markets greater flexibility and strengthen incentives for productivity. Rates may eventually fall, but nobody knows when. The country should prepare for capital to remain expensive long enough to expose overextended finances and unproductive investment. Cheap money once allowed policymakers to postpone hard decisions. That era is receding. Korea no longer has the luxury of tolerating low productivity, reckless leverage or misdirected capital. The task now is to make every unit of capital yield measurable return before higher borrowing costs turn into a permanent drag on growth. 저금리는 놀랍도록 오랜 기간 지속되었다. 이제 그 종말을 부인하기 어려워지고 있으며, 자본이 계속 저렴할 것이라는 가정 위에 지어진 정책들을 한국이 재검토하도록 강요하고 있다. 이번 주 미국 10년물 국채 수익률이 5퍼센트를 넘어섰고, 연방준비제도는 기준금리를 25bp 올려 3.75~4퍼센트로 인상했다. 이는 2023년 7월 이후 처음이다. 20년이 넘는 기간 동안 저렴한 자본, 에너지, 노동력은 경제가 그렇지 않으면 비용이 많이 들 수 있는 비효율성을 흡수하도록 도왔다. 이 완충 작용이 축소되면서 금리가 곧 옛날의 낮은 수준으로 돌아올 것이라는 기대를 중심으로 정책을 짜는 것을 멈춰야 한다. 장기 수익률은 단기 인플레이션보다 많은 요인의 영향을 받고 있다. 배럴당 100달러를 넘는 유가는 중동 분쟁이 지속되면서 물가 압력을 가중시키고 있다. 인공지능 인프라에 쏟아지고 있는 막대한 자금도 세계적 저축 자금을 놓고 경쟁하고 있다. 미국의 재정정책도 또 다른 압박 요인이다. 정부 채무가 국내총생산의 110퍼센트를 넘어섰고, 투자자들은 장기 국채를 보유하기 위해 더 큰 프리미엄을 요구하고 있다. 미국채가 과거에 누렸던 매우 유동적이고 안전한 자산으로서의 특별한 이점도 약화되었다.

유혹적인 지름길이 있다. 정부는 오늘날의 높아진 장기 수익률을 고정하는 것을 피하기 위해 더 많은 단기 채무를 발행할 수 있다. 하지만 이는 단지 문제를 더 가깝게 가져올 뿐이다. 더 많은 채무가 더 빨리 만기를 맞으면 금리가 높게 유지될 경우 재정 조달이 더 비싸진다. 채권 시장에 가격에 민감한 참여자와 레버리지가 높은 참여자가 더 많아지는 투자자 기반의 변화로 인해 기준 수익률이 더욱 불안정해질 수 있다.

한국도 이미 충격을 느끼고 있다. 10년물 국채 수익률이 4.6퍼센트를 넘어 2022년 10월 이후 최고 수준에 도달했다. 정부 채권 수익률의 상승은 결국 기업의 차입 비용과 은행 대출 금리로 흘러들어가 기업과 가계를 압박한다. 한국은행도 긴축 기조를 취해 7월과 8월 연이틀 기준금리를 3퍼센트까지 인상했다. 이는 2023년 1월 이후 처음 있는 연이틀 인상으로, 당시 한은은 2022년 4월에 시작된 인상 사이클을 완료했었다. 연방준비제도와의 금리 차이가 1퍼센트포인트까지 벌어졌으며, 약세 원화와 가계 부채의 높은 수준이 부담을 더하고 있다.

그러나 단순히 연방준비제도의 모든 움직임에 맞추는 것은 잘못된 통화정책이 될 것이다. 한국은행은 추가 인상을 위한 명확한 조건을 설정하고 국내 인플레이션, 환율, 신용 여건에 맞춰 그 시점을 판단해야 한다. 가계 신용이 이미 2,000조 원을 초과했고, 기업 부채도 그 규모에 가까워지고 있다. 높아진 이자 비용은 이를 감당할 여유가 거의 없는 차용자들에게 가장 큰 부담이 될 것이다. 금융 지원은 따라서 선별적이어야 한다. 대출을 무한정 연장하는 것은 손실을 해결하기보다는 감춘다.

재정정책도 자신의 부담을 안고 있다. 대규모 정부 차입은 시장 금리에 추가적인 상승 압력을 가할 수 있으며, 이자 지급이 예산에서 점점 더 많은 부분을 차지한다. 한국은 기초 재정 안정성을 지키기 위해 불필수적인 지출을 삭감해야 한다.

자본이 비쌀 때 경쟁력은 각 단위의 투자가 생산해내는 산출량에 달려 있다. 이는 시장 진입 장벽을 낮추고 노동 시장에 더 큰 유연성을 부여하며 생산성 인센티브를 강화하는 규제 개혁을 요구한다. 금리는 결국 떨어질 수 있지만 누구도 언제 그럴지 알 수 없다. 나라는 자본이 과도하게 부채를 진 금융과 생산성 낮은 투자를 드러낼 충분히 오랜 기간 동안 비싼 상태로 남을 가능성에 대비해야 한다. 저금리는 한때 정책 입안자들이 어려운 결정을 미룰 수 있게 했다. 그 시대는 지나가고 있다. 한국은 더 이상 낮은 생산성, 무모한 차입, 잘못된 자본 배분을 용인할 여유가 없다. 이제 할 일은 높아진 차입 비용이 경제 성장에 영구적인 걸림돌이 되기 전에 자본의 각 단위가 측정 가능한 수익을 내도록 하는 것이다.

editorials.title: Costly capital
editorials.body: Higher borrowing costs demand reforms that lift productivity, strengthen finances Cheap money has enjoyed a remarkably long run. Its retirement is now harder to deny, forcing South Korea to rethink policies built around the assumption that capital will remain cheap. This week, the 10-year US Treasury yield broke above 5 percent while the Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 3.75 to 4 percent, its first increase since July 2023. For more than two decades, cheap capital, energy and labor helped economies absorb inefficiencies that otherwise would have been costly. As that cushion shrinks, the nation should stop building policy around the expectation that rates will soon return to their old lows. Long-term yields are being shaped by more than near-term inflation. Oil above $100 a barrel is adding to price pressures as conflict persists in the Middle East. The vast sums being poured into artificial intelligence infrastructure are also competing for global savings. US fiscal policy is another strain. Gross public debt has climbed above 110 percent of gross domestic product, and investors are demanding a larger premium to hold long-dated government bonds. The special advantage once enjoyed by Treasurys as exceptionally liquid and safe assets has also weakened. There is a tempting shortcut. Governments can issue more short-term debt to avoid locking in today's elevated long-term yields. But that merely brings the problem closer. With more debt maturing sooner, refinancing becomes costlier if rates stay high. A changing investor base, with more price-sensitive and leveraged participants in bond markets, can make benchmark yields more volatile. Korea is already feeling the shock. The 10-year Treasury bond yield has risen above 4.6 percent, reaching its highest level since October 2022. Higher government bond yields eventually feed into corporate borrowing costs and bank lending rates, squeezing businesses and households. The Bank of Korea has also tightened, raising its policy rate to 3 percent over two consecutive meetings in July and August. It was the first back-to-back tightening since January 2023, when the BOK completed a rate-hike cycle that began in April 2022. The gap with the Fed has widened to as much as 1 percentage point, with a weaker won and heavy household leverage adding to the strain. Yet simply matching every Fed move would be poor monetary policy. The BOK should set clear conditions for further increases and weigh their timing against domestic inflation, exchange rates and credit conditions. Household credit has already exceeded 2,000 trillion won ($1.45 trillion), and corporate debt is nearing that scale. Higher interest expenses will weigh most heavily on borrowers with little room to absorb them. Financial support should therefore be selective. Extending loans indefinitely can conceal losses rather than resolve them. Fiscal policy faces its own burden. Large-scale government borrowing can put further upward pressure on market rates, and interest payments consume more of the budget. Korea should trim nonessential spending to preserve primary fiscal stability. When capital is expensive, competitiveness depends on the output generated by each unit of investment. That calls for regulatory reform to lower barriers to market entry, give labor markets greater flexibility and strengthen incentives for productivity. Rates may eventually fall, but nobody knows when. The country should prepare for capital to remain expensive long enough to expose overextended finances and unproductive investment. Cheap money once allowed policymakers to postpone hard decisions. That era is receding. Korea no longer has the luxury of tolerating low productivity, reckless leverage or misdirected capital. The task now is to make every unit of capital yield measurable return before higher borrowing costs turn into a permanent drag on growth.
